examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient Using Leibniz Notation
examples.worked_solution:
Let $u=1$ and $v=3x+7.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =0\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\eqalign{
			\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}	& = \dfrac{ v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}-u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}}{v^2}\
										& = \dfrac{ \left( 3x+7 \right ) \cdot 0 -1\cdot 3}{\left( 3x+7\right)^2}\
										& = -\dfrac{3}{\left( 3x+7\right)^2}.
		}
$$

In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=sin⁡x.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x)^{′}\cdot sin⁡x-x\cdot (sin⁡x)^{′}}{{(sin⁡x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot sin⁡x-x\cdot cos⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{sin⁡x-xcos⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$
